title: New Zealand Races to Vaccinate Endangered Birds After First H5N1 Case
excerpt: The country is rushing to protect 300 breeding birds from five critically endangered species in a rare vaccination programme after H5N1 bird flu was detected for the first time on its shores.
body:
• New Zealand detected its first H5N1 bird flu case on July 15 in a brown skua seabird near Wellington, followed by a second case in a native swamp harrier hawk two days later.
  • Health officials are vaccinating 300 breeding birds from five critically endangered species — kākāpō, takahē, shore plover, black stilt, and orange-fronted parakeet — in a programme few countries have attempted.
  • Poultry producers have begun moving free-range hens indoors in a voluntary "flockdown," while the government warns of potential egg and chicken shortages if the virus reaches commercial farms.
  • Oceania was the last region free of H5N1 until June 2026, when Australia reported its first case in a migratory seabird.

New Zealand confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu on July 15 after a brown skua — a subantarctic seabird — tested positive on a beach near Wellington. Two days later, a swamp harrier hawk in the North Island's Wairarapa region became the first native bird infected with the deadly strain, according to Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard.

The discoveries have triggered an emergency vaccination campaign targeting some of the country's rarest creatures. Health officials are now inoculating 300 core breeding birds from five critically endangered species: the kākāpō, takahē, shore plover (tchūriwat'), black stilt (kakī), and orange-fronted parakeet (kākāriki karaka).

A World-First Vaccination Programme

The Department of Conservation completed a world-first research trial last year showing vaccination is safe and effective in the five target species. The programme, approved by the Ministry for Primary Industries, uses a vaccine containing dead virus that cannot cause infection.

"We're in a unique position to be able to vaccinate some of our most vulnerable birds as a precaution," said Dr Kate McInnes, DOC's senior science adviser and wildlife veterinarian. "We've seen the devastating impacts of this virus on wildlife in other parts of the world, and we want to reduce the risk to our precious native birds where we can."

The kākāpō — a flightless nocturnal parrot with a total population of just 235 — faces particular risk because most of the species lives on one tiny island sanctuary off Stewart Island, where seabirds regularly pass through. The takahē, a ground-dwelling bird that was thought extinct until its rediscovery in 1948, is similarly vulnerable.

The iconic kiwi was notably left off the initial vaccination list. Ash Murray, DOC's biosecurity manager, explained that kiwi number around 70,000 and don't generally congregate in large groups. The rarest breeds — the rowi and Haast tokoeka — will likely be included in the next phase.

"These birds are only found in New Zealand; they're not found anywhere else in the world, so it's important to us."

— Andrew Hoggard, New Zealand Biosecurity Minister

Poultry Industry Locks Down

With only two infected wild birds detected so far — both found alive — New Zealand has moved swiftly onto a war footing. Some poultry producers have voluntarily moved free-range hens indoors in what the industry is calling a "flockdown." Auckland Zoo has cancelled close-encounter penguin experiences, and the Ōamaru penguin colony now requires visitors to disinfect their shoes on arrival.

"Some species might not notice it at all, and some will die in large numbers," warned Mary van Andel, the Ministry for Primary Industries' chief veterinary officer.

Hoggard has warned that if the virus reaches commercial poultry, mass culling would follow — the same strategy deployed globally. In the United States alone, at least 174 million chickens have been killed to contain outbreaks. Supermarkets have already begun cautioning customers not to panic buy eggs and chicken.

Millions of Years of Isolation at Stake

New Zealand's birds are uniquely vulnerable. The country's isolated islands had no predatory mammals for millions of years, allowing a remarkable array of flightless, ground-nesting species to evolve. Since human arrival roughly 700 years ago, more than a fifth of native bird species have been wiped out by introduced predators like stoats, rats, and feral cats.

More than half of the 93 endemic species that remain are considered to be "in serious trouble," according to government assessments. H5N1 could compound existing threats for populations already pushed to the brink.

""It won't be possible to vaccinate all endangered birds if bird flu arrives," Dr McInnes acknowledged."

The virus spreads primarily through droppings and saliva of infected birds, putting species that gather in large coastal colonies at greatest risk. In June, scientists revealed H5N1 had killed an estimated 13,000 seal pups on subantarctic islands southwest of Australia — three-quarters of the pup population there.

What Comes Next

Oceania had been the world's only region free of the deadly H5N1 strain until June, when an infected seabird was found on a Western Australian beach. Australia has since reported 14 confirmed or presumed detections.

New Zealand officials say being the last country to face H5N1 has given them years to prepare — a "massive advantage," in Murray's words. The Department of Conservation has worked with iwi (indigenous Māori groups), species recovery teams, and conservation organisations to develop response plans.

But there is no illusion that the virus can be stopped. "It won't be possible to vaccinate all endangered birds if bird flu arrives," Dr McInnes acknowledged. The focus will be on protecting the most vulnerable breeding populations and strengthening predator control programmes to give native species the best possible chance of weathering the outbreak.
image_caption: A kākāpō, one of five critically endangered New Zealand bird species being vaccinated against H5N1 bird flu. The flightless nocturnal parrot has a total population of just 235, most living on a single offshore island sanctuary.
